script.opening: "I’ve come up with these really sore red lumps on the fronts of both my shins over the last few days — they’re hot and tender to touch, and now they look a bit bruised. I’ve felt a bit fluey and my joints ache. I had a sore throat a couple of weeks ago. What on earth are they?"

facts.text: Five days. About six on the fronts of both shins, size of a 10p to a 50p coin, raised, red-purple, hot and very tender. The oldest ones look like bruises now. None have burst or wept. Will show them to the camera: shiny red-purple swellings on both shins.
Felt fluey, temperature 37.8 at home. Ankles ache and look a bit puffy. No rash elsewhere. Sore throat 2 weeks ago, settled on its own; no antibiotics.
No cough, no breathlessness, no night sweats, no weight loss. No diarrhoea, no blood in stools, no tummy pain. No red or painful eyes. No mouth ulcers. No recent travel. No TB contacts she knows of.
Started the combined pill 3 months ago (Microgynon). No antibiotics recently. Last period 3 weeks ago; "could I be pregnant? I don’t think so" — not using condoms as well. No allergies.
Fit and well; no asthma or stomach problems. Works as a nursery nurse — on her feet all day. Non-smoker, drinks socially. Lives with her boyfriend. Family: aunt has Crohn’s disease.

Alarmed — the bruised look frightened you. You thought they might be bites. Ask "Why would that matter?" if asked about the pill or pregnancy, and "An X-ray, for lumps on my legs?" if a chest X-ray is suggested. Reassured by a clear explanation that they will settle.

ice.ideas: "I thought maybe bites, or I’d knocked them. Now I don’t know."
ice.concerns: "They look like bruises — I looked up bruising on the legs and it said leukaemia." Worried about missing work.
ice.expectations: "Find out what they are and get something for the pain."

cues: "I had a sore throat a couple of weeks ago" — a possible trigger.
"Now they look a bit bruised" — her fear of a blood disorder.
"I started the pill a few months ago" (if medicines are asked about) — a possible cause.

checkpoints.text: Recognises ERYTHEMA NODOSUM — tender, warm, red-violet nodules on the shins, usually bilateral, non-ulcerating, resolving like bruises, often with fever/malaise/arthralgia — as a clinical diagnosis (panniculitis)

Recognises EN is REACTIVE and prioritises the search for an UNDERLYING CAUSE — streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, IBD, TB, drugs (oestrogen-containing contraceptives/sulfonamides), pregnancy, other infections; many no cause found; Löfgren’s syndrome — rather than only treating the legs
Takes a focused history for the causes (recent sore throat/infection, GI symptoms/weight loss, respiratory/eye symptoms, TB risk/travel, drugs incl. the pill, pregnancy)

Arranges a sensible work-up — ASOT (throat swab only if still sore), FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP/ESR, and importantly a CHEST X-RAY (sarcoid/TB), pregnancy test, with directed tests (calcium/ACE, calprotectin/GI, TB testing) per history

Manages the EN SUPPORTIVELY (self-limiting — rest, leg elevation, compression; NSAID only once pregnancy is excluded and with caution if IBD is suspected) and TREATS/REFERS for the underlying cause as found
Reassures about the skin lesions (self-limiting, not dangerous in themselves) while explaining that they are a clue to look for an internal cause, and addresses her alarm
Explains the diagnosis and the reason for the work-up (especially the chest X-ray) in accessible terms and checks understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: results review (especially CXR), what systemic symptoms warrant earlier review (weight loss, persistent cough, GI bleeding), supportive measures and expected resolution, and treatment/referral for the cause — recognising EN + the underlying-cause screen, not just treating the legs

worked.txt: "These are a recognised condition called erythema nodosum — tender, bruise-like lumps from inflammation in the fat under the skin, classically on the shins, and they go through that bruised look as they settle. The good news is the lumps themselves are not dangerous and usually clear over a few weeks."
"Here’s the key thing, though: these lumps are often a REACTION to something else going on in the body, so my main job is to find out why. Your recent sore throat is actually a common trigger."

"Let me ask a few things — any tummy upset, diarrhoea or blood, any cough or breathlessness, weight loss, recent travel or TB contact? And are you on the contraceptive pill, or could you be pregnant? These point to the different causes."

"I’d like to see the lumps in person to confirm this. I’ll do some bloods, including one for a recent strep throat infection, and importantly a chest X-ray — because two of the causes, sarcoidosis and TB, show up there. I’ll add a pregnancy test and anything else your answers point to."

"For the lumps themselves: rest, put your legs up and support stockings help, and they’ll fade on their own. Anti-inflammatory painkillers can help too, once we know you’re not pregnant and there are no bowel symptoms; otherwise paracetamol. We don’t need anything dramatic for the skin."

"Once the results are back we’ll know if there’s a cause to treat — like the throat infection — or to look into further. Come back sooner if you lose weight, develop a persistent cough, or get tummy symptoms. Let’s review with the X-ray and bloods."

f.learning: ERYTHEMA NODOSUM is a panniculitis presenting as crops of TENDER, warm, erythematous-to-violaceous NODULES on the SHINS (anterior lower legs), usually bilateral, which do NOT ulcerate and resolve like BRUISES over a few weeks, often with low-grade fever, malaise and arthralgia — a clinical diagnosis. The critical point is that EN is a REACTIVE condition, so the key task is to search for an UNDERLYING CAUSE rather than only treat the legs: streptococcal infection (a recent SORE THROAT is a common trigger), SARCOIDOSIS, INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE, TUBERCULOSIS, DRUGS (notably oestrogen-containing contraceptives and sulfonamides), PREGNANCY, and TB and other infections, with many cases (about a third) having no cause found; EN with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, fever and ankle arthritis is LÖFGREN’S SYNDROME, an acute sarcoidosis that usually settles (BTS 2021). Take a focused history aimed at these causes (recent infection/sore throat; GI symptoms, diarrhoea, blood, weight loss — IBD; respiratory/eye symptoms — sarcoid; TB risk/travel/contacts; current drugs, especially the pill; pregnancy), and arrange a sensible work-up after a face-to-face examination: ASO titre (a throat swab only if the throat is still sore), FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP/ESR, and importantly a CHEST X-RAY (for sarcoidosis — bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy — and TB), a pregnancy test, and directed tests per history (calcium/ACE if sarcoid suspected, faecal calprotectin/GI work-up for bowel symptoms, TB testing if at risk) — the chest X-ray being a high-yield, easily-forgotten investigation. Manage the EN itself supportively, as it is usually self-limiting (rest, leg elevation, compression; an NSAID only once pregnancy is excluded and with caution in suspected IBD, BNF), and treat or refer for the underlying cause as found. The hidden agenda is wanting to know "what are they"; reassure about the skin lesions while conducting the underlying-cause screen including a chest X-ray, not only treating the legs.

knowledge.guideline: [1] BTS Clinical Statement on pulmonary sarcoidosis (British Thoracic Society, 2021) · [2] NICE NG33 (tuberculosis, 2016) · [3] NICE NG84 (sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018) · [4] NICE NG129 (Crohn’s disease, 2019) and NICE NG130 (ulcerative colitis, 2019) · [5] NICE HTG320 (formerly DG11; faecal calprotectin testing, 2013)
knowledge.summary: Tender, warm, red-purple nodules on both shins that fade like bruises, with fever and aching joints two weeks after a sore throat, is erythema nodosum. The lumps settle on their own over weeks; the task is to look for the cause. Take a targeted history, check bloods including an ASO titre and a pregnancy test, and always request a chest X-ray for sarcoidosis and TB. Treat symptoms with rest, elevation and an NSAID once pregnancy is excluded.

points.t: A septal panniculitis: tender, warm, raised red or violet nodules, usually on both shins, which do not ulcerate and fade through bruise colours over about 3–6 weeks without scarring. Fever, malaise and arthralgia often come first or alongside. It is a clinical diagnosis.

points.h: It is a reaction — find the trigger
points.t: Common triggers in the UK: streptococcal throat infection, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, drugs (notably oestrogen-containing contraceptives and sulfonamides), pregnancy, and TB and other infections. Many cases have no cause found.

Erythema nodosum with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, fever and ankle arthritis is Löfgren’s syndrome, an acute form of sarcoidosis that usually settles; the chest X-ray is what finds it [1]. Ask about cough, breathlessness and red or painful eyes.
Ask about cough, night sweats, weight loss, contact with TB, and birth in or travel to high-incidence countries. A chest X-ray and specialist referral are needed if TB is possible (NICE NG33 [2]).

FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP or ESR, ASO titre (a throat swab is only useful if the throat is still sore; NICE NG84 [3] covers treatment), pregnancy test, and a chest X-ray. Add calcium and ACE if sarcoidosis is suspected, faecal calprotectin if bowel symptoms (NICE HTG320 [5]), and TB testing if at risk.

Rest, leg elevation and support; an NSAID such as naproxen or ibuprofen for pain once pregnancy is excluded, with caution in suspected IBD, peptic ulcer or renal disease (BNF). Stop a likely culprit drug.

Dermatology if the diagnosis is uncertain, lesions ulcerate, or they recur or persist beyond about 6–8 weeks. Respiratory for hilar nodes or lung changes, gastroenterology for suspected IBD (NICE NG129, NG130 [4]), TB services if TB is possible.

Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.

model.text: Hello Ms Marsden, I’m Dr Clarke. What’s brought you in today?

I’ve come up with these really sore red lumps on the fronts of both shins over the last few days. They’re hot and tender, and now they look a bit bruised. I’ve felt fluey and my joints ache. I had a sore throat a couple of weeks ago. What on earth are they?
That sounds painful and worrying. I’ll ask a few questions, have a look, and then explain what I think they are and what we need to do. Is that okay?
Yes, fine.
Did you bang your legs, or get bitten? Have any of the lumps opened or wept?
model.why: Excludes trauma and bites; checks for ulceration

model.text: No, nothing like that. They haven’t broken.
Tell me more about the sore throat. Has it gone now?
Yes, it’s gone now.

Some other things can trigger lumps like these, so I’ll run through a few. Any cough or breathlessness, or red or painful eyes? Any tummy pain, diarrhoea or blood in your stools? Night sweats or weight loss?
No, nothing like that. I’ve just felt achy and a bit feverish.
Have you been in contact with anyone with TB, or travelled anywhere recently?
Not that I know of.
Are you on any medicines at the moment, including the pill? And is there any chance you could be pregnant?
Why would that matter?
Both hormones and pregnancy can set these off, and it also affects which painkillers are safe. I’ll go through your medication record with you, and I’d like to do a pregnancy test to be sure.
model.why: Explains the reason and plans a pregnancy test

model.text: That’s fine.
What have you been thinking they might be?
I thought maybe bites, but now they look bruised I got scared it’s something serious.
That’s an understandable worry when things look like bruises. What were you hoping we’d do today?
Find out what they are and get something for the pain.
Can I look at your legs? … These are tender, warm, raised lumps under the skin on both shins, and some are fading purple. I’ll also check your temperature, throat, glands, chest and joints.
model.why: Examines the lesions and looks for systemic clues

model.text: What are they?

They’re called erythema nodosum. It’s inflammation in the fat layer under the skin. The good news is they aren’t dangerous, don’t scar, and fade like bruises over a few weeks. They aren’t a sign of anything dangerous in themselves.
model.why: Names it and addresses the specific fear

model.text: Oh, thank goodness. So why have I got them?

That’s the key question. These lumps are the body reacting to something else. Your sore throat is the most likely trigger, but they can also come from things like sarcoidosis, a bowel condition, TB, some medicines or pregnancy. So rather than just treating your legs, I want to find the trigger.
model.why: Explains the reactive nature and the need to find a cause

model.text: I’d like blood tests, including one that shows a recent strep throat, inflammation markers, kidney and liver tests, and a pregnancy test. And a chest X-ray, which is important because it can show sarcoidosis or TB, even when you feel well in your chest.
model.why: Bloods with ASO titre, pregnancy test and chest X-ray

model.text: An X-ray, for lumps on my legs?
It sounds odd, I know. One common cause is sarcoidosis, which often shows up as swollen glands in the chest together with lumps like these and aching joints. The X-ray is the simplest way to find it.
model.why: Explains why the chest X-ray matters

model.text: Okay, that makes sense.

For the pain, rest with your legs raised and a supportive stocking can help. Once the pregnancy test is negative, an anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen or naproxen works well. Until then, paracetamol is the safe option. Is that okay for you?
model.why: Supportive care; NSAID only after pregnancy excluded

model.text: Yes. Should I be resting?

Rest while they’re sore. If you can’t manage work, the first week is self-certified and I can do a fit note after that. I’ll ring you with the results, and if we find a cause we’ll treat it or refer you to the right team.
model.why: Practical support and a clear plan for results

model.text: Please get back to me sooner if you develop a cough or breathlessness, painful red eyes, diarrhoea or blood in your stools, night sweats or weight loss, if any lump breaks open, or if you feel much more unwell. If the lumps haven’t faded in six to eight weeks, or keep coming back, I’ll refer you to dermatology. Can you tell me what the plan is?
model.why: Specific safety net, referral threshold and teach-back

model.text: Bloods, pregnancy test and a chest X-ray. Paracetamol until the test is negative, then ibuprofen, legs up. Come back if I get a cough, eye or bowel problems, or they don’t go.
Spot on. I’ll see you in about two weeks to go through the results.

social.t: Standing and walking hurt. Ask about her job and offer a fit note if needed beyond seven days (self-certification covers the first seven).
Bruise-like lesions frighten people. Name the fear and explain early that the lumps themselves are harmless and fade, while the tests look for the trigger.

legal.t: Self-certification for up to seven days; a fit note after that if she is not fit for work, with adjustments such as seated duties.

professional.t: Make a clear plan for who checks and communicates the chest X-ray and blood results, and when (GMC Good medical practice).
If TB is suspected, refer to the TB service; TB is a notifiable disease and the diagnosing clinician notifies UKHSA.

community.t: SarcoidosisUK for patient information if sarcoidosis is found; Crohn’s & Colitis UK if IBD is found.

redFlags: Cough, breathlessness, red painful eyes — sarcoidosis
Night sweats, weight loss, TB contact or travel — TB
Diarrhoea, blood in stool, abdominal pain — IBD
Ulcerating or atypical lesions — reconsider the diagnosis
psychosocial: Pain affecting daily activities and work
ice: Expectation: a diagnosis and pain relief

playbook.diagnosis: Erythema nodosum, most likely post-streptococcal given the sore throat two weeks ago, with low-grade fever and arthralgia. Sarcoidosis (including Löfgren’s syndrome), IBD, TB, drugs and pregnancy to be excluded.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s called erythema nodosum — inflammation in the fat under the skin. It isn’t dangerous and fades like a bruise over a few weeks. It’s the body reacting to something, most likely your sore throat, so we’ll check for other triggers too.”

management.reflectIce: “You were frightened this was something serious because they look like bruises. The lumps themselves aren’t dangerous — and the tests are how we make sure nothing else is going on.”
management.psychosocial: Fit note if needed; reassurance about the natural course.
sharedPlan: FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP or ESR, ASO titre, pregnancy test
Chest X-ray for sarcoidosis and TB
Rest, elevation, support; paracetamol, then an NSAID once pregnancy is excluded (BNF)
Stop any culprit drug; treat or refer the cause found
safetyNet: Return for cough, breathlessness, eye pain, bowel symptoms, night sweats, weight loss or ulceration
Dermatology if persistent beyond 6–8 weeks or recurrent
Results review in about two weeks

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by treating the legs and forgetting the patient. The nodules are a signpost; the marks are for following it.

items.why: Bilateral tender shin nodules with fever and arthralgia are erythema nodosum.
items.fix: Recognise the pattern and name it.

items.why: Sarcoidosis and TB are key causes and the X-ray is how they are found.
items.fix: Request a chest X-ray in every new case.

items.fail: Prescribing an NSAID before checking for pregnancy.
items.why: Pregnancy is a trigger and NSAIDs should be avoided in pregnancy.

items.fail: Not asking about bowel, eye or chest symptoms.
items.why: These point to IBD or sarcoidosis.

items.fail: Missing her fear of something serious.
items.why: It is the concern she brought.
items.fix: Ask what she thought and answer it directly.

items.fail: No plan for results or persistence.
items.why: The cause may only show on tests; persistence needs referral.
items.fix: Set a results review and a dermatology threshold.

wordPics.fail: Calls it cellulitis and gives antibiotics; or names erythema nodosum and just gives ibuprofen with no search for a cause; no chest X-ray; no pregnancy test before NSAIDs.
wordPics.pass: Recognises erythema nodosum; screens causes; requests bloods, ASO titre and a chest X-ray; supportive treatment; safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: explains clearly why a chest X-ray is needed for leg lumps; addresses her fear of something serious; checks pregnancy before NSAIDs; knows Löfgren’s syndrome; clear results plan and referral routes; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s a skin infection — here’s a course of antibiotics.”
avoid.instead: “These are erythema nodosum, a reaction under the skin. I want to find what triggered it.”
avoid.why: Misdiagnosis as cellulitis treats the wrong problem and misses the cause.

avoid.dont: “Take ibuprofen and they’ll go on their own.”
avoid.instead: “They will fade, but I need to find the trigger — including a chest X-ray.”
avoid.why: The skin settles by itself; the marks are for the underlying-cause screen.

avoid.instead: “Paracetamol for now, and an anti-inflammatory once the pregnancy test is negative.”
avoid.why: Pregnancy is a trigger and NSAIDs should be avoided in pregnancy (BNF).

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] BTS Clinical Statement on pulmonary sarcoidosis (British Thoracic Society, 2021) · [2] NICE NG33 (tuberculosis, 2016) · [3] NICE NG84 (sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018) · [4] NICE NG129 (Crohn’s disease, 2019) and NICE NG130 (ulcerative colitis, 2019) · [5] NICE HTG320 (formerly DG11; faecal calprotectin testing, 2013)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Tender, warm, red-purple nodules on both shins that fade like bruises, with fever and aching joints two weeks after a sore throat, is erythema nodosum. The lumps settle on their own over weeks; the task is to look for the cause. Take a targeted history, check bloods including an ASO titre and a pregnancy test, and always request a chest X-ray for sarcoidosis and TB. Treat symptoms with rest, elevation and an NSAID once pregnancy is excluded.

points.t: A septal panniculitis: tender, warm, raised red or violet nodules, usually on both shins, which do not ulcerate and fade through bruise colours over about 3–6 weeks without scarring. Fever, malaise and arthralgia often come first or alongside. It is a clinical diagnosis.

points.h: It is a reaction — find the trigger
points.t: Common triggers in the UK: streptococcal throat infection, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, drugs (notably oestrogen-containing contraceptives and sulfonamides), pregnancy, and TB and other infections. Many cases have no cause found.

Erythema nodosum with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, fever and ankle arthritis is Löfgren’s syndrome, an acute form of sarcoidosis that usually settles; the chest X-ray is what finds it [1]. Ask about cough, breathlessness and red or painful eyes.
Ask about cough, night sweats, weight loss, contact with TB, and birth in or travel to high-incidence countries. A chest X-ray and specialist referral are needed if TB is possible (NICE NG33 [2]).

FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP or ESR, ASO titre (a throat swab is only useful if the throat is still sore; NICE NG84 [3] covers treatment), pregnancy test, and a chest X-ray. Add calcium and ACE if sarcoidosis is suspected, faecal calprotectin if bowel symptoms (NICE HTG320 [5]), and TB testing if at risk.

Rest, leg elevation and support; an NSAID such as naproxen or ibuprofen for pain once pregnancy is excluded, with caution in suspected IBD, peptic ulcer or renal disease (BNF). Stop a likely culprit drug.

Dermatology if the diagnosis is uncertain, lesions ulcerate, or they recur or persist beyond about 6–8 weeks. Respiratory for hilar nodes or lung changes, gastroenterology for suspected IBD (NICE NG129, NG130 [4]), TB services if TB is possible.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her describe the lumps, the flu-like illness and the sore throat before narrowing.
Asked about work and the effect of the pain; explored drugs, pregnancy, travel and TB contacts.
Picked up the recent sore throat as the likely trigger and the fear that the bruising meant something serious.
Idea: bites. Concern: something serious. Expectation: a diagnosis and pain relief.
Examined the lesions, temperature, throat, lymph nodes, chest and joints; bloods with ASO titre, pregnancy test and chest X-ray.
Erythema nodosum versus cellulitis, bites, vasculitis and bruising; triggers: strep, sarcoid, IBD, TB, drugs, pregnancy.
Screened respiratory, eye, bowel and TB symptoms; weight loss and night sweats; ulceration.
Erythema nodosum, likely post-streptococcal, with the cause still to be confirmed.
Rest, elevation, support; paracetamol, then an NSAID once pregnancy is excluded; stop any culprit drug; treat or refer the cause.
Pregnancy and possible IBD considered before NSAIDs; fit note if needed; referral routes by cause.
Return for cough, eye, bowel or systemic symptoms or ulceration; dermatology if persistent over 6–8 weeks or recurrent; results review in two weeks.

social.t: Standing and walking hurt. Ask about her job and offer a fit note if needed beyond seven days (self-certification covers the first seven).
Bruise-like lesions frighten people. Name the fear and explain early that the lumps themselves are harmless and fade, while the tests look for the trigger.

legal.t: Self-certification for up to seven days; a fit note after that if she is not fit for work, with adjustments such as seated duties.

professional.t: Make a clear plan for who checks and communicates the chest X-ray and blood results, and when (GMC Good medical practice).
If TB is suspected, refer to the TB service; TB is a notifiable disease and the diagnosing clinician notifies UKHSA.

community.t: SarcoidosisUK for patient information if sarcoidosis is found; Crohn’s & Colitis UK if IBD is found.

redFlags: Cough, breathlessness, red painful eyes — sarcoidosis
Night sweats, weight loss, TB contact or travel — TB
Diarrhoea, blood in stool, abdominal pain — IBD
Ulcerating or atypical lesions — reconsider the diagnosis
psychosocial: Pain affecting daily activities and work
ice: Expectation: a diagnosis and pain relief

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Erythema nodosum, most likely post-streptococcal given the sore throat two weeks ago, with low-grade fever and arthralgia. Sarcoidosis (including Löfgren’s syndrome), IBD, TB, drugs and pregnancy to be excluded.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “It’s called erythema nodosum — inflammation in the fat under the skin. It isn’t dangerous and fades like a bruise over a few weeks. It’s the body reacting to something, most likely your sore throat, so we’ll check for other triggers too.”

management.reflectIce: “You were frightened this was something serious because they look like bruises. The lumps themselves aren’t dangerous — and the tests are how we make sure nothing else is going on.”
management.psychosocial: Fit note if needed; reassurance about the natural course.
sharedPlan: FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP or ESR, ASO titre, pregnancy test
Chest X-ray for sarcoidosis and TB
Rest, elevation, support; paracetamol, then an NSAID once pregnancy is excluded (BNF)
Stop any culprit drug; treat or refer the cause found
safetyNet: Return for cough, breathlessness, eye pain, bowel symptoms, night sweats, weight loss or ulceration
Dermatology if persistent beyond 6–8 weeks or recurrent
Results review in about two weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by treating the legs and forgetting the patient. The nodules are a signpost; the marks are for following it.

items.why: Bilateral tender shin nodules with fever and arthralgia are erythema nodosum.
items.fix: Recognise the pattern and name it.

items.why: Sarcoidosis and TB are key causes and the X-ray is how they are found.
items.fix: Request a chest X-ray in every new case.

items.fail: Prescribing an NSAID before checking for pregnancy.
items.why: Pregnancy is a trigger and NSAIDs should be avoided in pregnancy.

items.fail: Not asking about bowel, eye or chest symptoms.
items.why: These point to IBD or sarcoidosis.

items.fail: Missing her fear of something serious.
items.why: It is the concern she brought.
items.fix: Ask what she thought and answer it directly.

items.fail: No plan for results or persistence.
items.why: The cause may only show on tests; persistence needs referral.
items.fix: Set a results review and a dermatology threshold.
